in.rationale: Burns et al. define PGR as the fraction of the performance gap between the weak and strong ceiling models that is recovered with weak supervision. They report a ceiling estimate of +14.1 for their Elicitation ∪ Complementary estimate versus +11.2 for the previous ground-truth elicitation estimate; the cited passages do not show whether this higher estimate is achievable.

Lang, Huang and Li define PGR with the same formula, so their PGR values are on Burns et al.'s scale.

in.other_title: Wen et al. adopt a Best-of-N Performance Recovered (PR) metric following Burns et al.'s framework
in.rationale: Burns et al. define performance gap recovered relative to a weak-supervisor baseline and a strong ceiling; the authors explicitly build on that framework but define PR as a ratio to the Pass@N oracle, without a weak-model baseline. PR scores Best-of-N sampling guided by reward models trained on critics' judgments (in the Figure 3 setting, on a fixed 7B supervised model with critic models of varying sizes, which the passage does not say are weaker), whereas PGR scores a weak-to-strong model trained with weak supervision against the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: How to measure how much of a model's achievable performance a supervision signal recovers; Burns et al. use weak supervision, while the authors use reward models trained on the judgments of critics of varying sizes.

text: The authors define performance gap recovered (PGR) as the fraction of the performance gap between the weak and strong ceiling models that is recovered by training with weak supervision, i.e. (weak-to-strong minus weak) divided by (strong ceiling minus weak).
